posts.excerpt: The best fintech teams design with constraints, not around them.
posts.body:
Every product team building in financial services eventually hits the same wall: a compliance requirement that seems to demand an extra screen, an extra disclosure, an extra moment of friction. The reflex is to treat this as a tax on the experience — something to minimise, hide, or apologise for. That reflex is usually wrong.

Constraints are not the opposite of good design; they're raw material for it. A KYC step framed as bureaucracy feels like an obstacle. The same step framed as "here's exactly what we're checking and why" becomes a moment of trust-building, because the user finally understands what the system is doing with their information and why it matters.

The teams that get this right treat legal and design as one conversation from the start, not two conversations stitched together at the end. When a compliance officer and a designer sit in the same room early, the resulting flow tends to need fewer screens, not more — because the constraint gets solved once, structurally, instead of being patched over repeatedly.

There's a pattern I keep seeing in wealth and lending products: the disclosure nobody reads isn't a UX failure, it's a sign the disclosure was treated as a legal artifact rather than a product surface. Rewriting it in plain language, breaking it into the moments where it's actually relevant, and giving people a real choice rather than a single "I agree" checkbox does more for both compliance and conversion than any redesign of the surrounding screens.

None of this means every constraint is secretly a gift. Some are genuinely painful, and part of the job is pushing back on the ones that exist only because "that's how it's always been filed." But the default posture matters. Start from what the rule is protecting, not from how to route around it, and the resulting product is usually both safer and clearer — which, in financial services, is really the same thing said twice.
posts.pullquote: The best fintech teams design with constraints, not around them.
posts.title: Compliance isn't the enemy of good UX

posts.excerpt: Sometimes the roadmap's best item is what gets removed.
posts.body:
A few quarters ago I sat through a roadmap review where the most celebrated line item was a new comparison tool — three tabs, filterable, exportable. It shipped, and usage was fine. But the metric that actually moved that quarter was a different change entirely: we deleted a settings page that had accumulated nine toggles over two years, six of which fewer than 1% of users had ever touched.

Removing things doesn't get a launch announcement. It doesn't have a demo. But every option a product carries is a decision the team is asking someone else to make on every visit, and most of those decisions were made once, for one client, in one meeting, and never revisited.

The audit that led to that deletion was simple: for every configurable setting, we asked who changed it in the last twelve months, and whether the product broke in any meaningful way if the answer was "basically nobody." Where the answer was genuinely nobody, we removed it and watched support tickets, not vanity metrics, for two weeks.

What's worth noticing is why those settings existed at all. Almost none were requested by users. They were requested by a stakeholder anticipating an objection, or added defensively after a single complaint, or left over from a migration where nobody wanted to make the call to drop them. Each one was reasonable in isolation. Together, they were the reason new users needed a walkthrough just to get started.

A roadmap with a deletion on it looks unambitious in a planning meeting and looks exactly right three months later, when the product is easier to explain, easier to support, and — if anyone's counting — easier to sell.
posts.pullquote: Sometimes the roadmap's best item is what gets removed.
posts.title: The feature that should have been a deletion

posts.excerpt: Every new integration quietly adds a decision the user has to make.
posts.body:
Partnership growth in fintech has a particular shape: it compounds business value quickly and compounds product complexity even faster, and the two curves rarely get reviewed together. Every new partner integration is sold internally as "just another option in the flow," and each one, taken alone, is a reasonable addition.

The trouble shows up after the fifth or sixth partner, when a user who once had a single clear path now faces a decision the product was never designed to explain: which provider, which rate, which fine print. Nobody chose to build a confusing product. It accumulated, one shipped partnership at a time.

The fix isn't to slow down partnerships — the commercial logic behind them is usually sound. It's to separate the decision the business needs (more optionality, more coverage, more routes to revenue) from the decision the user is being asked to make in the interface. Often that means the product should choose a sensible default on the user's behalf and expose the alternatives only when they materially matter, rather than surfacing every partner as an equal, unexplained option.

This requires product and business development to share a single view of what's actually driving outcomes, updated as partnerships are added — not a retrospective UX cleanup once the flow has become unmanageable. The healthiest fintech platforms I've worked with review their integration surface on the same cadence they review new partnerships, so the two never drift more than a quarter apart.

The test I use is simple: could someone new to the product explain, in one sentence, why they're seeing this option instead of another? If the honest answer requires knowing the company's partnership history, the interface is carrying weight it shouldn't be carrying, and the fix belongs in the product, not in a longer help article.
posts.pullquote: Every new integration quietly adds a decision the user has to make.
posts.title: Partnerships scale faster than product clarity

posts.excerpt: Independence only feels safe when the product removes doubt.
posts.body:
"Self-directed" is often used as a synonym for "minimal." Give someone raw data, a search bar, and an order ticket, and call it empowerment. In practice, the products that earn real usage from first-time independent investors do the opposite: they add more structure, not less, at the exact moments where doubt is highest.

Independence isn't the absence of guidance — it's the presence of enough context that a person trusts their own decision. A DIY platform that only shows a price chart is asking someone to supply all the judgment themselves. A DIY platform that surfaces why a price moved, what a reasonable range of outcomes looks like, and what similar investors with similar goals tend to do, is still self-directed, but far less lonely.

The failure mode I see most often is founders equating "advice" with "liability" and stripping out anything that resembles guidance, on the theory that a bare interface is legally and philosophically safer. It's rarely true. Well-designed educational context — clearly separated from personalised advice — reduces both anxiety and the kind of impulsive, regret-prone decisions that create support tickets and churn.

This shows up concretely in onboarding. First-time investors don't drop off because a product is too complicated to operate; they drop off because they don't trust their own understanding of what they're about to do. The products that convert best treat the first transaction as a teaching moment, not a funnel step — confirming, in the user's own words where possible, what they believe is about to happen before it happens.

The goal isn't to make independent investing feel like it's being done for the user. It's to make the moment of independence feel earned rather than assumed — closer to handing someone the keys after they've driven with you in the passenger seat than to handing them the keys on day one and wishing them luck.
posts.pullquote: Independence only feels safe when the product removes doubt.
posts.title: What "DIY investing" actually requires from a product

posts.excerpt: Every extra field is a small bet against the user finishing.
posts.body:
Treat an onboarding flow as a form and you'll optimise it like one: fewer fields, shorter labels, a progress bar. Those changes help, but they miss what's actually happening in a financial product's onboarding, which is a sequence of trust decisions disguised as data entry.

Every field asks a small, implicit question: does this person trust us enough to tell us this yet? Income before the user understands what it's for. A permanent account number before the value of the product has been demonstrated. Each of these can be technically necessary and still be sequenced badly, asked before the trust required to answer honestly has been built.

The teams that get onboarding right map the flow not by field type but by trust cost — which pieces of information feel invasive relative to what's been explained so far. Reordering a flow so the highest-trust-cost fields come after a moment of demonstrated value, rather than before it, routinely improves completion more than removing fields does.

This also changes how error states should be designed. A validation failure early in a high-trust-cost field reads as the product doubting the user before it's earned the right to; the same failure later, after some rapport has been established, reads as a normal correction. The error message is identical. The trust context around it is not.

None of this argues for delaying legitimate requirements. It argues for being deliberate about the order in which a product asks for things, and honest about which fields exist for the user's benefit versus the business's. A form gets you compliance. A sequence of earned trust gets you a completed application from someone who still feels good about the company on the other side of it.
posts.pullquote: Every extra field is a small bet against the user finishing.
posts.title: The onboarding screen is a trust decision, not a form

posts.excerpt: Most metrics on screen are there for the builder, not the user.
posts.body:
Open most financial dashboards and you'll find the same failure repeated: a dozen figures competing for the same square inch of attention, each one defensible, none of them decisive. The dashboard isn't wrong so much as it's answering the wrong question — it's showing everything the system can measure instead of the one or two things the person in front of it actually needs to decide something.

Most of those extra numbers didn't arrive because a user asked for them. They arrived because an internal stakeholder wanted visibility into something they cared about, and the path of least resistance was to add a card to the dashboard rather than build a separate reporting view. Multiply that by a few product cycles and you get a screen that serves the org chart better than it serves the person using the product.

The fix starts with a blunt exercise: for a given user, what is the one decision this screen exists to support, and what is the smallest set of numbers that changes that decision? Everything else belongs one click away, not zero clicks away. This is uncomfortable in a review, because it means telling a stakeholder their favourite metric isn't earning its place on the primary surface — but the alternative is a dashboard that answers no question well because it's trying to answer all of them equally.

There's a related trap worth naming: precision dressed up as clarity. A number carried to two decimal places looks rigorous, but if the user's decision doesn't change between 4.31% and 4.3%, the extra digit is noise wearing the costume of insight. Rounding appropriately is itself a design decision, and it's usually the more honest one.

The best dashboards I've worked on got there by subtraction, not addition — a handful of true redesigns that mostly involved removing things nobody could quite explain, and giving the two or three numbers that remained enough visual room to actually be read.
posts.pullquote: Most metrics on screen are there for the builder, not the user.
posts.title: Why your dashboard has too many numbers
